literal: From the grandfather Verus: good-character and freedom-from-anger.
prose: From my grandfather Verus I learned good character and freedom from anger.

literal: From the reputation and the memory concerning the [one who] fathered [me]: the modesty and the manliness.
prose: From the reputation and memory of my father: modesty and manliness.

literal: From the mother: the piety and generosity and abstaining not only from doing-wrong, but also from the coming-to-be of such a thought: further then, the simplicity with regard to the way-of-life and far from the wealthy lifestyle.
prose: From my mother: piety and generosity, and abstaining not only from doing wrong but even from entertaining such a thought. She also taught me simplicity in one's way of living, far removed from the manner of the rich.

literal: From the great-grandfather: the [lesson] not into public lecture-courses to attend, and the [lesson] with good teachers with-regard-to house to make-use-of, and the [lesson] to recognize that into such-things one-must unstintingly be-spending.
prose: From my great-grandfather: not to have attended public schools, but to have had good teachers at home, and to recognize that on such things one ought to spend unstintingly.

literal: From the tutor: the not either a-Greens-partisan nor even a-Blues-partisan nor even either a-Parmularius-supporter or a-Scutarius-supporter to become: and the toil-enduring and content-with-little: and the self-sufficiency and unmeddlesomeness: and the slowness-to-accept of-slander.
prose: From my tutor: not to become a devoted partisan of the Greens or the Blues at the races, nor a supporter of the Parmularius or Scutarius gladiators in the arena; to endure toil and to need little; to work with my own hands and not meddle in others' affairs; and to be slow to accept slander.

literal: From Diognetus: the not-wasting-zeal-on-vain-things: and the being-skeptical toward the things said by the miracle-working and charlatan ones concerning incantations and concerning the exorcism of spirits and of such other things told: and the not to-keep-quails-for-fighting nor also to-be-excited about such things: and the to-endure of-frankness-of-speech: and the to-become-devoted to-philosophy and the to-attend first indeed of-Baccheius, then of-Tandasis and of-Marcianus: and the to-write dialogues in childhood: and the to-desire a-camp-bed-frame and a-pallet-skin and as-many-such-things as belong-to the Greek training.
prose: From Diognetus: not to waste my enthusiasm on trifles; to be skeptical of the claims made by miracle-workers and charlatans about incantations, the exorcism of spirits, and other things of that sort; not to keep quails for fighting, nor to be excitedly absorbed in such pursuits; to tolerate frankness of speech; to become devoted to philosophy, and to attend first the lectures of Baccheius, then those of Tandasis and Marcianus; to write dialogues in my childhood; and not to long for a camp-bed, a pallet-skin, or any of the other things that belong to the Greek discipline of education.

literal: From Rustics: the to-take an-impression of-the needing of-correction and of-treatment of-the character: and the not to-be-turned-aside into a-sophistic rivalry, nor the to-write-treatises concerning the theorems, or exhortatory little-discourses to-deliver, or in-a-fantasy-struck-manner the ascetic or the practical man to-display-oneself-as.
prose: From Rusticus: to grasp the impression that my character needed correction and treatment; also, not to turn aside into a sophist's zeal for rivalry, not to write treatises on abstract doctrines, not to deliver little exhortatory speeches, and not to make a showy display of oneself as an ascetic or a man of action, in a manner obsessed with impressing others.

literal: And to abstain from rhetoric and from poetry and from elegant-wordplay: and the not in formal-attire at home to walk about, nor to do such things: and the letters simply to write, such as the [letter] by this man himself to my mother written from Sinuessa:
prose: To abstain from rhetoric, poetry, and elegant wordplay; not to walk about at home in formal dress, nor to do things of that sort; and to write letters in a simple, unaffected style, like the one he himself wrote to my mother from Sinuessa.

literal: And the toward-those having-grown-angry and having-erred easily-recalled and easily-reconciled: whenever most-quickly they-themselves should-wish to-return, to-be-disposed; and the accurately to-read and not to-be-satisfied considering-around wholly, nor to-those talking-around quickly to-assent; and the to-encounter the Epictetean notes, of-which from-his-own-house he-shared[-with-me].
prose: To be easily called back and easily reconciled toward those who had grown angry with me or wronged me, as soon as they themselves were willing to return to good terms; to read carefully and not be satisfied with a general, superficial grasp of a matter, nor to give quick assent to those who talk glibly around it; and to encounter the notes on Epictetus, which he shared with me from his own household.

literal: From Apollonius: the freedom and unwaveringly unrisked-to-chance, and to look to nothing else, not even for a little, or with a view to reason: and the [being] always alike, in sharp pains, in loss of a child, in long illnesses: and on a living example to see plainly that the same man is able to be most vehement and relaxed:
prose: From Apollonius: to be free and unwaveringly steadfast, never looking to anything else, even for a moment, except to reason; to remain always the same, in sharp pains, in the loss of a child, and in long illnesses; and to see clearly, from a living example, that the same man can be both utterly intense and relaxed.

literal: And the not-being-irritable in the explanations: and the to-see-a-man clearly deeming [himself] least of-his-own excellences [in] the experience and the skill, the one concerning the transmitting the theorems: and the to-learn how it-is-necessary to-receive the seeming favors from friends, neither being-overcome on-account-of these-things, nor insensibly passing-[them]-by.
prose: Not to be irritable when giving explanations; also to have seen a man who clearly considered his experience and skill in transmitting his theoretical knowledge to others as the least of his own excellences; and to learn how one ought to accept apparent favors from friends, neither being overcome by them so as to compromise oneself, nor passing them by unfeelingly.

literal: From Sextus: the kindliness: and the example of the household being-ruled-by-a-father: and the concept of the according-to-nature living: and the dignity unaffectedly: and the perceptiveness of friends caringly: and the tolerance of the laymen and the unobservant-disregard of-those-thinking [they have insight]:
prose: From Sextus: kindliness; the example set by a household governed by a father's rule; the concept of living according to nature; to cultivate dignity without artifice; to size up friends with real perceptiveness, and to do so with genuine care for their welfare; and to tolerate ordinary people, even those who think without any insight at all.

literal: And the toward all-men agreeableness: so-that of-all flattery more-pleasant to-be the company of-him, and most-respected to-those-same in that very time to-be:
prose: Also his gracious manner toward everyone, so agreeable that his company was more pleasant than any flattery, and yet at the very same time most respected by those very people in his presence.

literal: And the never to display any expression of anger or of some other passion, but at once indeed to be most free-from-passion, and at once most full-of-tender-affection: and the well-spokenness unostentatiously, and the wide-learnedness without display.
prose: Never to display any trace of anger or other passion, but to be at once utterly free from passion and yet full of tender affection; and to be well-spoken without ostentation, and widely learned without display.

literal: From Alexander the grammarian: the not-being-faultfound and the not reproachfully to-lay-hold-of those-who brought-forward something barbarous or solecistic or ill-sounding, but skillfully that very thing only, that which it-was-needful to-have-been-said, to-bring-forward, in manner of-an-answer or of-a-joint-testifying or of-a-joint-consideration concerning the very matter, not concerning the word, or through some other of-that-kind tactful side-reminder.
prose: From Alexander the grammarian: not to be faultfinding, and not to rebuke reproachfully those who uttered some barbarism, solecism, or ill-sounding phrase, but skillfully to bring forward just that very expression which ought to have been said, in the form of an answer, or a corroborating testimony, or a joint consideration of the matter itself, not of the word, or through some other such tactful indirect reminder.

literal: From Fronto: to take note what-sort-of the tyrannical envy and duplicity and hypocrisy, and that as for-the-most-part the called these among us well-born-men are somehow rather-lacking-in-affection.
prose: From Fronto: to take note of the sort of envy, duplicity, and hypocrisy that characterize a tyrant, and that, as a general rule, those among us who are called well-born are somehow rather lacking in natural affection.

literal: From Alexander the Platonist: not often nor without necessity to say to someone or in a letter to write that busy I-am, and not through this the manner continually to-excuse-oneself-from the with-regard-to the toward those living-with relations fitting-duties, putting-forward-as-excuse the surrounding affairs.
prose: From Alexander the Platonist: not often, nor without necessity, to say to someone or write in a letter that I am too busy, and not to use this way of continually excusing myself from the duties owed by one's relations toward those one lives with, by pleading the pressing business that surrounds one.

literal: From Catulus: the not carelessly to-hold [it] when-a-friend is-complaining about-something, even if he-should-happen complaining unreasonably, but to-try to-restore [him] to the accustomed [footing]: and the concerning the teachers ardently favorable-speaking, such-as the things concerning Domitius and Athenodotus being-recorded: and the concerning the children truly loving [disposition].
prose: From Catulus: not to regard a friend's complaint lightly, even if he happens to complain unreasonably, but to try to restore him to his usual footing; and to speak favorably and warmly about my teachers, as in the anecdotes recorded about Domitius and Athenodotus; and a truly loving disposition toward her children.

literal: From the brother of-me Severus: the love-of-family and love-of-truth and love-of-justice; and the through him to-come-to-know Thrasea, Helvidius, Cato, Dio, Brutus, and to-take a-thought of-a-constitution based-on-equality, administered according-to equality and equal-freedom-of-speech, and of-a-kingship valuing most of-all-things the freedom of-those being-ruled.
prose: From my brother Severus: love of family, love of truth, and love of justice; and through him I came to know Thrasea, Helvidius, Cato, Dio, and Brutus, and formed a conception of a constitution based on equality and equal freedom of speech, and of a kingship that values above all else the freedom of the governed.

literal: And still from the same [one]: the evenness and the steadfastness in the honor [she showed]; and [I learned] the beneficence and the generosity earnestly, and the good-hope and the trustfulness concerning being-loved by [my] friends; and [I learned] the undisguised toward those happening to fall under condemnation by him; and [I learned] not to need conjecture of his friends about what he wants or what he does not want, but to be plain.
prose: She also taught me, further, the evenness and steadfastness she maintained in honoring others, and to be ready to do good, to give generously, to hope for the best, and to trust confidently that I was loved by my friends; and to be open and undisguised toward those who happened to fall under his censure; and not to need to guess at what his friends wanted or did not want, but to make it plain to them myself.

literal: From Maximus: the mastering of oneself and in nothing to be swayed-about: and the good-humor both in the other circumstances and in the illnesses: and the even-temperedness of the character, and gentle and dignified: and the not-complainingly effective [ability] of the-things lying-before [him]:
prose: From Maximus: to master myself and never be swayed this way and that by anything; to remain good-humored both in other circumstances and in illness; the even temper of his character, blended with gentleness and dignity; and his effectiveness in working through the tasks before him without complaint.

literal: And the [belief] of-all in-him to-believe about-the-things-which he-might-say that so he-thinks, and about-the-things-which he-might-do that not badly he-does: and the freedom-from-wonder and freedom-from-consternation and nowhere hurrying or hesitating or being-at-a-loss or downcast or having-grinned-forcedly, or again growing-angry or being-suspicious:
prose: Also to make everyone believe that he really thought as he spoke, and that whatever he did, he did it with no ill intent; and to be free from wonder and free from consternation, never in a hurry about anything, nor hesitant, nor at a loss, nor downcast and forcing a grin, nor again prone to anger or given to suspicion.

literal: And the beneficence and the readiness-to-forgive and the freedom-from-falsehood: and to provide an impression of one unbent rather than one being-corrected: and that no one would ever have thought himself to be despised by him, nor would he have endured to suppose anyone better than himself: and the being-graciously-witty.
prose: Also his beneficence, his readiness to forgive, and his freedom from falsehood; and to present the appearance of a character naturally unbent rather than one merely corrected; and that no one could ever have thought himself despised by him, nor would he have endured supposing anyone to be better than himself; and to be graciously witty.

literal: From the father: the gentleness and steadfastness unshakably upon the things judged after-careful-examination; and the freedom-from-vanity regarding the seeming honors; and the industriousness and persistence; and the readiness-to-listen of-those having something of-public-benefit to-bring-forward; and the unswervingly apportioning to-each according-to merit; and the [skill] skilled where indeed [there is] need of-tension, and where [there is need] of-relaxation.
prose: From my father's memory: gentleness, and to remain unshaken and steadfast in decisions that have been carefully examined; freedom from vanity regarding things that seem to be honors; to be industrious and persistent; readiness to listen to anyone who had some contribution of public benefit to bring forward; to distribute to each according to merit without ever swerving from it; and the skill of knowing where there is need for tension and where for relaxation.

literal: And to stop the things concerning the loves of the: young men. And community-of-mind, and the having-been-granted to friends, not indeed to dine-together with him always, nor to travel-abroad-together compulsory, but always him to be regarded the same by those on-account-of some need left-behind: and the being-inquiring exactly in counsels and persistent, but not the standing-off-too-soon from investigation, having-been-satisfied with the ready-at-hand impressions: and the maintaining of friends and nowhere fickle nor frantic: and the self-sufficiency in everything, and the cheerfulness.
prose: And to stop the passions for boys. Also community of mind: to let one's friends off, not requiring them always to dine with one or invariably to travel abroad together, but always regarding one in the same way toward those left behind on account of some pressing need. Also to be exact and persistent in inquiry when giving counsel, and not to abandon an investigation prematurely, content with the impressions that first present themselves. And to maintain steadfast loyalty toward friends, nowhere becoming fickle or fanatically attached. She also taught me self-sufficiency in everything, and cheerfulness.

literal: And the from-far-off foreseeing and of-the-smallest-things forearranging without-tragic-display: and the acclamations and all flattery upon herself suppression, and the watchfulness ever of-the-necessities for-the-rule and stewardship of-the-provision, spending unstintingly on such things, and endurance of-the over-certain-such-things blame-incurring: and the not indeed concerning-gods superstition, nor indeed concerning-people popularity-seeking or fawning or crowd-pleasing, but sobriety in all-things and steadfastness and nowhere lacking-in-taste nor yet innovation-loving:
prose: She also taught me to plan far ahead and to make provision even for the smallest matters, without theatrical fuss; to suppress popular acclaim and all flattery directed at herself; to be ever watchful over the necessities of rule; to be a careful steward of expenditure, spending unstintingly on such things, and to endure the blame incurred for such carefulness; and not to be superstitious about the gods nor, in dealings with people, to court popularity, curry favor, or please the crowd, but rather to be sober-minded in all things, steadfast, nowhere lacking in taste, and not given to novelty for its own sake.

literal: And the that-not-ever-anyone-could-say: neither that sophist, nor that home-bred-slave, nor that pedant, but that [he was] a man ripe, complete, unflattered, being able to manage both the [things] of-himself and of-others.
prose: And also that no one could ever call him a sophist, a home-bred slave, or a pedant, but rather a mature man, a complete one, immune to flattery, and capable of managing both his own affairs and those of others.

literal: Toward these things: and the esteem of those truly philosophizing, but toward the others not reproachful nor indeed easily-led-astray by them: further then: the sociability and graciousness, not excessively: and the caring-for of [one's] own body in due measure, neither as one would be fond-of-life nor for adornment, nor indeed carelessly, but so-that through [one's] own attentiveness to have need of very few things of medicine, or of drugs and poultices from outside:
prose: Besides these things, she also had genuine esteem for those who truly practice philosophy, while toward the others she was neither reproachful nor easily led astray by them. She also taught me sociability and graciousness, without excess, and to care for one's own body in due measure, neither as one overly fond of life nor for the sake of adornment, yet not carelessly either, but so attentive to it that through such personal care one had very little need of medicine, or of drugs and poultices from outside.

literal: Especially and the yielding-without-envy without-envy to-those possessing some ability, such-as the expressive [ability] or the [ability] from study of-laws or of-customs or of-other certain matters, and being-eager-along-with them, so-that each according-to their own merits might-be-well-esteemed: doing all-things according-to the ancestral [ways], yet not this same [thing] cultivating to-appear, [namely] the guarding the ancestral [ways].
prose: Above all, the readiness to yield without envy to those who possessed some special ability, such as skill in expression, or knowledge derived from the study of laws, customs, or other matters, and to join eagerly in supporting them, so that each might win esteem according to his own particular merits; and to do everything in accordance with ancestral custom, yet without making a show of cultivating that very custom, but simply guarding ancestral ways.

literal: Further then: the not easily-moved and given-to-flitting, but even in-places and in-affairs the same given-to-abiding [being].
prose: She also taught me not to be easily shaken or given to flitting about, but to be steadfast, dwelling on the same places and the same activities.

literal: Not at-unseasonable-hours a-bather, not fond-of-building, not about foods a-deviser, not about garments' weaves and colors, not about bodies' beauty: the from-Lorium robe leading-up from the lower villa: a-tunic at Lanuvium the-many-times [times]: to-the-one begging-off from-the-cloak at Tusculum, how he-made-use, and every the of-that-kind manner.
prose: Not to bathe at unseasonable hours; not to be fond of building; not to be fastidious about food, or about the weave and color of clothing, or about the beauty of bodies; the toga from Lorium, the robe worn on the way up from the lower villa; the simple tunic worn at Lanuvium, for the most part; and how he behaved toward the man at Tusculum who begged off from lending his cloak, and how every such manner naturally behaves.

literal: Nothing harsh, not indeed implacable, not violent, not so-that anyone ever to-say [of her anything of the sort]: until sweat. But all things having-been-allotted to-be-reckoned as at leisure, undisturbedly, in-orderly-fashion, vigorously, harmoniously with-themselves. And would-suit him the concerning Socrates being-remembered [thing], that both to-abstain and to-enjoy he-was-able of-these-things, of-which the many in-relation-to both the abstinences weakly and in-relation-to the enjoyments indulgently are-disposed.
prose: Nothing harsh, nor indeed implacable, nor violent, nor such that anyone could ever say of her anything of the sort: to persist to the point of sweat. But she taught me that all things are to be reckoned as having their allotted places, as though at leisure, without disturbance, in good order, vigorously, and in harmony with one another. What is remembered of Socrates would suit him: that he was able both to abstain from and to enjoy those things in relation to which most people are weakly disposed toward abstaining and self-indulgently disposed toward enjoying.

literal: The being-strong and enduring and being-sober in-each-alike: of-a-man it-is, sound and unconquered soul possessing, such-as in the illness the [illness] of-Maximus.
prose: To be strong, to endure, and to remain sober in either fortune is the mark of a man possessing a soul at once sound and unconquered, such as his was in the illness of Maximus.

literal: From the gods: the [having] good grandfathers, good parents, a good sister, good teachers, good household-members, kinsmen, friends almost all to have; and that concerning none of them did you fall-before into doing-wrong anything, although having such a disposition, from which, if it chanced, even I would have done something of that kind; and of-the gods [it was their] kindness—the [fact] that no confluence of affairs came-to-be, which was-going to expose me.
prose: From the gods: to have good grandfathers, good parents, a good sister, good teachers, good household members, kinsmen, and friends—almost all of them; and that concerning none of them did I fall before into any wrongdoing, although I had such a disposition that, had the chance arisen, I might well have done something of that sort; but it was the gods' kindness that no confluence of circumstances ever arose that was going to expose me.

literal: And not to be brought up further with the mistress of my grandfather: and to preserve the youth: and not before due time to be made-a-man, but still even to take hold of the time.
prose: Not to be brought up too long in my grandfather's household with his mistress; to preserve my youthful purity; and not to be made a man before the proper time, but even to delay it a while longer.

literal: The to-a-ruler and to-a-father to-be-subjected: who was-about all the vanity to-strip-away of-me and into a-thought to-bring of-the [fact] that possible it-is, in a-court living, not indeed of-bodyguards to-need, nor of-conspicuous garments, nor of-lamps and of-such-certain statues and of-the similar display, but it-is-permitted very-nearly to-a-private-citizen to-reduce oneself, and not on-account-of this more-lowly or more-remiss to-hold with-a-view-to the [things] on-behalf-of the common-interests in-a-manner-befitting-a-leader to-be-done, [things] which-must [be done].
prose: To be subject to a ruler and father who was bound to strip away all my vanity and bring me to the realization that it is possible to live in a court without needing a bodyguard, or conspicuous garments, lamps, statues, and the like display, but that one can reduce oneself very nearly to the condition of a private citizen without thereby becoming meaner or more remiss regarding the things that must be done authoritatively on behalf of the common interest.

literal: The [thing], to chance upon such a brother: one being able on the one hand through character to rouse me toward care of myself, and at the same time also delighting me with honor and with affection: the [thing], children to me not to come to be without natural gifts nor distorted with regard to the little body: the [thing], me not to have advanced further in rhetoric and poetics and the other pursuits, in which perhaps I would have been held fast, if I had perceived myself advancing easily.
prose: To have had such a brother, one able through his character to rouse me to care for myself, and at the same time to delight me with the honor and affection he showed me: my children not to be born without natural gifts, nor deformed in body: not to make further progress in rhetoric, poetry, and the other pursuits, in which I might perhaps have become absorbed, had I perceived myself advancing easily in them.

literal: The to-outrun the tutors in honor to-establish, of-which indeed they-seemed to-me to-desire, and not to-postpone in-hope of-the me, since young still we-were, later this-same-thing doing: the [lesson] to-know Apollonius, Rusticus, and Maximus.
prose: Not to outrun my tutors but to establish them in honor, as they seemed to me to desire, and not to postpone doing this in the hope, since we were still young, that I would do it later: through them, to come to know Apollonius, Rusticus, and Maximus.

literal: The to-be-imagined concerning the according-to-nature of-life clearly and often such-as someone is, so-that, as-much-as depends on the gods and on the from-there dispensations and cooperations and inspirations: nothing hinders now according-to-nature to-live me, but to-fall-short still of-this through the my-own fault and through the not diligently-keeping the from the gods remindings and almost teachings:
prose: To form a vivid and frequent picture of what a life according to nature is like, so that, as far as depends on the gods and the dispensations, cooperations, and inspirations that come from them, nothing should any longer prevent me from living according to nature; and yet I still fall short of this through my own fault, and through not diligently keeping the reminders—almost the very teachings—that come from the gods.

literal: The [my] body to hold out for me to such an extent in such a life: not to have touched either Benedicta or Theodotus, but even later, having come to be in erotic passions, to be sound: having become angry oftentimes at Rusticus, to do nothing more, in that in which I might have changed my mind: the [her], being about to die young, the one having borne me nevertheless to dwell with me the last years.
prose: That my body held out for so long in enduring such a life: that I never touched Benedicta or Theodotus, but even later, when caught up in erotic passions, recovered soundness of mind: that though I was often angry with Rusticus, I never went so far as to do anything I would afterward regret: that though destined to die young, she nevertheless chose to spend her last years living with me.

literal: The [being-well-supplied] with proper tutors for the children, to be well supplied [with].
prose: To be well supplied with proper tutors for my children, spending unstintingly on such things.

literal: The through dreams remedies to-be-given: both others and so-as not to-spit blood and not to-feel-dizzy, and of-this at Caieta just-as you-will-treat-yourself: the how I-desired philosophy: not to-fall into some sophist, nor to-sit-down to the composing-treatises or syllogisms analyzing or about the meteorological-matters occupying-myself: for all these-things of-gods helping and of-fortune require: The [things-written] among Quadi at the Granua.
prose: That remedies were given through dreams, among others, both against spitting blood and against dizziness, and also, at Caieta, an oracle telling how you would be treated, just as you were treated. That when I conceived a desire for philosophy, I did not fall into the hands of some sophist, nor waste my time writing treatises, working out syllogisms, or occupying myself with speculations about the heavens. For all these things require the gods' help and fortune's favor as well. Written among the Quadi, on the river Granua.
